azure-policy-initiative.title: Azure Policy initiative definition structure – Microsoft Learn
azure-policy-initiative.notes: An Azure Policy initiative definition bundles several related policy definitions into one group that is assigned and managed as a single unit instead of assigning each policy separately. It is authored in JSON, and a typical example is collecting related tagging policies together. The structure contains a display name, description, policy type, optional metadata, a version, optional parameters and an array of the included policy definitions. Each entry in that array points to a built-in or custom policy by its ID, carries a short reference ID, can pass parameters through and may name a specific definition version. Versions follow a major, minor and patch scheme, and custom initiative versioning is still a preview feature. Parameters can have defaults, allowed values and a strong type that gives a picker in the portal. Groups inside an initiative map policies to controls and compliance domains for regulatory compliance standards such as NIST SP 800-53. Once an initiative is assigned, its parameters can no longer be changed, so setting default values is advised.

azure-private-5g-core.title: Azure Private 5G Core documentation – Microsoft Learn
azure-private-5g-core.notes: Azure Private 5G Core is documented as a service for deploying and managing private mobile networks for 5G IoT devices. The documentation hub is a landing page that lists topics rather than explaining them in running text, and it is marked as archived, so the content may no longer be current. Topics cover the key components and design requirements of a private mobile network, and deployment through the Azure portal, ARM templates, the command line and PowerShell. Further areas are network slices, sites and packet core instances including service plans and upgrades, and quality of service and traffic handling through policy control, services and SIM policies. SIM management covers provisioning and SIM groups. Monitoring topics mention Azure Monitor platform metrics, distributed tracing, packet core dashboards and event hub based usage data, while diagnostics topics include packet capture, ping and traceroute on the packet core instance. An AKS cluster has to be commissioned as part of the prerequisites. The page itself names no licensing details or numeric limits.

azure-private-dns-zone.title: What is Azure Private DNS? – Microsoft Learn
azure-private-dns-zone.notes: Azure Private DNS resolves and manages domain names inside virtual networks without requiring a custom DNS solution. A private DNS zone lets resources use custom domain names instead of the names Azure generates. Zone data is stored as a global resource and is not tied to one virtual network or region. A virtual network must be linked to a zone before it can resolve the zone's records, and linked networks do not need to be peered with each other. Autoregistration is enabled on the link and makes Azure create and keep current A records for virtual machines. Supported record types include A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT. A private zone may share its name with a public zone, which gives split-horizon DNS. Reverse lookups work only within the private address space of the linked network. A network with autoregistration can be linked to only one private zone, and the .local domain is discouraged. Conditional forwarding to on-premises DNS needs the Azure DNS Private Resolver.

azure-resource-locks.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure – Microsoft Learn
azure-resource-locks.notes: Management locks let administrators protect a subscription, resource group or resource from accidental deletion or modification. A lock overrides the permissions of users and roles, so it applies to everyone, unlike role-based access control. There are two levels: CanNotDelete, called Delete in the portal, allows reading and changing but not deleting, while ReadOnly allows only reading and behaves like the Reader role for everybody. Locks are inherited by child resources, including ones added later, and when several locks apply the most restrictive one wins. They cannot be placed on management groups. Locks act only on control-plane operations sent to the Resource Manager endpoint, not on data-plane operations, so they do not protect data inside, for example, a storage account or database. Creating or removing a lock requires Microsoft.Authorization permissions, which the Owner and User Access Administrator roles have. A ReadOnly lock can have surprising side effects, such as blocking listing of storage account keys or restarting virtual machines in a locked group.

azure-resource-tags.title: Tag resources, resource groups, and subscriptions for logical organization – Microsoft Learn
azure-resource-tags.notes: Azure tags are metadata key-value pairs, such as Environment set to Production, that are attached to resources, resource groups and subscriptions to organize them logically. They are not supported on management groups. Typical uses are grouping billing data by cost center or environment and making sure cost-generating services carry tags through policy. Tag names are case-insensitive for operations while tag values are case-sensitive. Applying tags needs either write access to the tags resource type, as in the Tag Contributor role, or write access to the resource itself, as in the Contributor role. Resources do not inherit tags from their resource group or subscription, so policy definitions are used to enforce or copy them. Each resource can hold a limited number of tag pairs, and name and value lengths are capped, with a tighter name limit for storage accounts. Some characters are forbidden in names, and certain services such as DNS, Traffic Manager and Front Door add their own restrictions. Classic resources are not supported. Tags are stored as plain text, so sensitive values should not be placed in them.

azure-routing-preference.title: What is routing preference? – Microsoft Learn
azure-routing-preference.notes: Routing preference defines how traffic travels between Azure and the internet: either over the Microsoft global network, which is cold potato routing, or over the ISP network and public internet, which is hot potato routing. The Microsoft global network is the default for all Azure services. The choice affects egress data transfer cost, and the internet option is positioned as the cost-optimized one. The preference is chosen when a public IP address is created and cannot be changed afterwards. With the Microsoft network option, traffic stays on Microsoft's backbone as long as possible and enters or leaves at an edge point close to the user. With the internet option, traffic exits Microsoft's network in the region hosting the service, while traffic inside Azure still uses the direct Microsoft WAN path. Internet routing works only with zone-redundant Standard SKU public IPv4 addresses and cannot be combined with NAT gateways or IP-based public load balancers. Supported resources include virtual machines, scale sets, AKS, Application Gateway and Azure Firewall. For storage accounts, primary endpoints always use the Microsoft network and only secondary endpoints can use the internet option. Availability is limited to listed regions.

azure-service-tags.title: Virtual network service tags – Microsoft Learn
azure-service-tags.notes: A service tag stands for a group of IP address prefixes belonging to a given Azure service. Microsoft maintains the prefixes and updates the tag automatically when addresses change, so administrators do not have to track IP ranges by hand. Tags can be used in network security group rules as source or destination, in Azure Firewall rules and in user-defined routes. A rule that names a tag such as Storage covers all current and future ranges of that service. Global tags span the whole cloud, while regional variants such as Storage with a region suffix narrow the scope, although not every tag supports regions. Some tags depend on others, for example AzureBackup needs Storage and Azure Active Directory. Service tags alone do not secure traffic, and AzureCloud includes addresses used by other Azure customers, so allowing it broadly is not recommended. Several tags cannot be used in routes, and the AzureLoadBalancer tag covers only health probe traffic. Ranges differ between clouds, and weekly JSON files plus a discovery API, PowerShell and CLI commands let on-premises firewalls retrieve them.

azure-sql-elastic-pool.title: Elastic pools help you manage and scale multiple databases in Azure SQL Database – Microsoft Learn
azure-sql-elastic-pool.notes: Elastic pools in Azure SQL Database manage and scale several databases that have varying and unpredictable usage. The databases sit on one server and share a fixed set of resources at a fixed price, which helps SaaS developers balance price and performance for a group of databases while each one can still burst. This avoids over-provisioning and under-provisioning. Resources are set with either the DTU model, using eDTUs, or the vCore model, and the combined usage of all databases decides what the pool needs. Optional minimum and maximum limits can be set per database, and databases or resources can be added or removed with little downtime. Elastic jobs can run scripts across the databases in a pool. Pooled databases keep single-database business continuity features such as point-in-time restore, geo-restore and failover groups. A logical server is required, and databases from different servers cannot share a pool. Billing is hourly for the pool itself based on its configured size, not per database. Pools suit many databases with low average load and occasional, staggered peaks, but not several databases with constantly high load.

azure-storage-redundancy.title: Azure Storage redundancy – Microsoft Learn
azure-storage-redundancy.notes: Azure Storage always keeps multiple copies of data to protect against hardware faults, network or power outages and major disasters, so that a storage account can meet its availability and durability targets. The choice trades lower cost against higher availability. Within the primary region, locally redundant storage copies data inside one datacenter, while zone-redundant storage replicates synchronously across several availability zones. Geo-redundant storage and geo-zone-redundant storage add an asynchronous copy in a paired secondary region, which is itself locally redundant. The read-access variants expose the secondary through an endpoint with a secondary suffix, and a customer-initiated account failover can promote the secondary. Because geo-replication is asynchronous, data can be lost if the primary region fails, and the recovery point objective describes that gap. Redundancy is configured per storage account, and the secondary region cannot be chosen freely. Replication does not guard against deletions or overwrites, since those are applied to every copy. Some options are unavailable for certain account types, the archive tier and unmanaged disks.

bi-center-of-excellence.title: Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap: Center of Excellence – Microsoft Learn
bi-center-of-excellence.notes: A data or analytics center of excellence is an internal team of technical and business experts that actively supports other people in the organization who work with data. It forms the core of the wider community effort to drive adoption and follows the data culture vision. It is also called a competency center or center of expertise, and many organizations let their BI team carry out these tasks. A formal place in the org chart is recommended but not required, as long as responsibilities are defined, prioritized and assigned. Typical activities include mentoring, office hours, co-development projects, best-practice reviews, maintaining a central portal, curating training material, providing templates, communicating governance guidelines, administering the platform and handling support escalations. Common roles are leader, coach, trainer, data analyst, data modeler, report creator, data engineer and user support. The page describes centralized, unified, federated and decentralized structures, each with trade-offs such as silos or competing priorities, and names unified or federated as usually most effective. Funding can follow a cost center model, a profit center model or a mix, and no specific licence is required for the team itself.

bicep-module.title: Bicep modules – Microsoft Learn
bicep-module.notes: A Bicep module is a Bicep file that another Bicep file deploys; it may also be an ARM template in JSON. Modules are meant to make files easier to read by hiding complex deployment details and to let the same building block be reused across deployments. During compilation they are converted into one ARM template that uses nested deployments. A module declaration has a symbolic name, a path to the file, an optional deployment name and a params block. Optional settings include a scope for deploying to a different resource group, subscription, management group or tenant, a condition, a loop for several instances, explicit dependencies and outputs. Modules can come from a local file, from the public registry that hosts Azure Verified Modules, from a private Azure Container Registry, or from a template spec, and aliases can be defined in a configuration file. Without declared dependencies, modules deploy in parallel. Registry delivery is supported only by Bicep, and template specs cannot package extra artifacts such as scripts. Secret values should be passed with the getSecret function.

bicep-what-if.title: Bicep deployment what-if operation – Microsoft Learn
bicep-what-if.notes: What-if is an Azure Resource Manager operation that previews the changes a Bicep deployment would make, without altering any existing resources. It works from Visual Studio Code, Azure PowerShell, Azure CLI, the REST API and the Azure SDKs, and at resource group, subscription, management group and tenant scope. The create commands accept a switch that shows the preview and asks for confirmation before deploying, and a JSON output option allows programmatic processing. The result lists each resource with a change type such as create, delete, modify, no change, ignore, no effect or deploy, shown with plus, minus and tilde symbols. Result format and validation level can be set, and deployment stacks can also be previewed. Permissions are the same as for deploying, meaning write access to the resources and rights on deployments. A local alternative, the bicep snapshot command, needs no Azure connection. The preview has limits: nested templates are expanded only up to certain bounds, linked template references are not evaluated, expressions such as newGuid, utcNow and reference are not resolved, and default values can show up as noise.

block-download-policy.title: Block download of files from SharePoint sites or OneDrive – Microsoft Learn
block-download-policy.notes: The block download policy lets a SharePoint administrator stop users from downloading files from a SharePoint site or OneDrive, without relying on Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies. The aim is to reduce the risk of data loss while people can keep working. It is turned on per site with the Set-SPOSite PowerShell cmdlet, not as an organization-wide setting. Affected users get browser-only access: downloading, printing and syncing are blocked, as is opening files in desktop Office apps, and moving files to other SharePoint sites, including through Power Automate. Optional parameters exclude site owners, specific groups or SharePoint groups, and can additionally make the site read-only. The policy can also be tied to a sensitivity label through label advanced settings. Prerequisites are those of SharePoint Advanced Management, including the SharePoint Online PowerShell module. Apps running in app-only mode, such as virus scanners and search crawlers, are exempt. Some Office apps, Power Apps and Power Automate may behave differently, so Microsoft suggests testing with a few users first.

claiming-partner-of-record.title: Submit a claim for Claiming Partner of Record – Microsoft Learn
claiming-partner-of-record.notes: Microsoft uses the Claiming Partner of Record model to manage associations between partners and customers who have Modern Work and Security or Business Applications workloads. The claims apply only to a short list of engagements, namely a business applications presales advisor engagement, Modern Work and Security usage, business applications usage recognition and business applications revenue. A partner creates a claim as a draft, attaches proof of execution such as a customer-signed statement of work, and submits it. Microsoft validates the claim, and the customer is notified and can decline it at any time. If it is not declined, the association to the tenant and workload becomes binding and the partner can see usage data for the associated products. A customer may have several partners, but each workload or subscription can be linked to only one. The submitter needs the incentives admin role, the partner ID, the customer's tenant ID and customer contact details. Partner roles differ by solution area and some are limited to volume licensing or CSP. CSP, managed reseller, hosting and Surface are not covered, and a submitted claim cannot be edited.

client-side-evaluation.title: Client vs. Server Evaluation – EF Core – Microsoft Learn
client-side-evaluation.notes: Entity Framework Core tries to evaluate a query on the server, that is, in the database, as far as possible. Parts of the query can become parameters evaluated on the client, and the database provider translates the rest into an equivalent database query. Partial client evaluation is supported only in the top-level projection, which is the last Select call. If that projection cannot be translated, EF Core fetches the required data and evaluates the remainder on the client. An untranslatable expression anywhere else, such as in a Where filter, causes a runtime exception, because it would require loading all data into memory. Developers can force client evaluation explicitly with AsEnumerable, AsAsyncEnumerable, ToList or ToListAsync, which suits small data sets or operators without a server translation. The streaming variants avoid buffering, while the list variants buffer and help when results are enumerated more than once. Client evaluation can hurt performance and can cause memory leaks when cached delegates capture instances such as a DbContext. Before EF Core 3.0, client evaluation was allowed anywhere in a query and only logged a warning.

code-component.title: Code components overview – Power Apps – Microsoft Learn
code-component.notes: Code components are solution components, built with the Power Apps component framework, that are packaged in a solution file and imported into different environments. They work in model-driven apps and canvas apps and also support Power Pages. After the solution is imported into a Dataverse environment, administrators and customizers can set up columns, subgrids, views and dashboard subgrids to use the component instead of the default one. A code component has three parts: a manifest, an XML file that names the component, states whether it binds to a field or a dataset, lists configurable properties and the resource files; an implementation written in TypeScript; and resources such as code, CSS, images and RESX files for localization. The implementation provides an init method, an updateView method, an optional getOutputs method and a destroy method. When a user changes data, the component calls notifyOutputChanged so the platform requests the outputs, and when the platform changes data it calls updateView. The Power Platform CLI creates the project through the pac pcf init command. The page names no licence requirements and no explicit technical limits.
